Star Wars (1977) – A Milestone in Film History That Has Lost Much of Its Shine Over Time Although Star Wars (1977) undoubtedly made cinematic history and had a lasting impact on an entire genre, it becomes increasingly difficult to fully understand the enthusiasm surrounding the film when watching it from a modern perspective. What was once considered a revolutionary science-fiction adventure now feels surprisingly outdated, drawn-out, and lacking in variety in several places. Of course, the film deserves recognition for its historical significance, but that does not make it immune to criticism of its numerous shortcomings. Let's start with arguably the most recognizable element of the film: its soundtrack. The iconic score is undoubtedly a classic and has long since become part of popular culture. However, it has become so omnipresent over the years that, at least for me, much of its original impact has worn off. It sometimes feels as though that one iconic musical theme is being blasted into our ears 24/7. What was once distinctive and impressive now feels almost excessively overused. The technical presentation also leaves a rather mixed impression. The image resolution feels somewhat lacking in places, while the outdated editing techniques further contribute to certain scenes feeling artificially drawn out. Especially when compared to modern film productions, it becomes apparent just how much cinematic technology and filmmaking techniques have evolved. What was considered spectacular in 1977, particularly the explosions and space battles, hardly inspires any excitement today. Much of it simply feels outdated and can no longer compete visually with contemporary productions. The action is particularly disappointing to me. The space battles frequently follow the same formula, repeating almost identical scenarios until they quickly become monotonous. At the same time, there is a noticeable lack of variety and genuine dynamism. The lightsaber duels are also nowhere near the level of modern fight choreography. They come across as simplistic, clumsy, and at times almost uninspired. On top of that, despite the relatively limited amount of action, some sequences are surprisingly difficult to follow. This creates a rather strange contradiction: overall, the film offers far too little action for my liking, yet it still fails to present the action sequences it does have in a consistently convincing and coherent manner. Another major point of criticism is the pacing. It fluctuates considerably between rushed sequences and unnecessarily drawn-out passages. Exciting situations are occasionally resolved far too quickly, while other scenes are needlessly prolonged through extended dialogue and largely irrelevant moments. The excessive screen time given to C-3PO and R2-D2 is particularly frustrating. C-3PO repeatedly gets caught up in lengthy monologues that do more to interrupt the narrative flow than to enrich it. R2-D2, meanwhile, does little to preserve my patience with his constant beeping and repetitive electronic noises. What was presumably intended as comic relief and a defining character trait increasingly turned into an auditory endurance test for me. More generally, the film often fails to resolve exciting situations in a particularly satisfying way. Instead of genuine suspense and compelling storytelling, we occasionally get surprisingly mundane and underwhelming solutions. The rather explicit presentation of certain scenes also makes it clear that the film belongs to a different era of filmmaking. This is not necessarily a bad thing in itself, but it becomes quite noticeable when compared to modern cinematic standards and audience expectations. Of course, it would be unfair to judge Star Wars exclusively by the standards of modern blockbusters while completely disregarding its historical context. The film undoubtedly set new standards, influenced the technological development of cinema, and gave rise to an extraordinary franchise. However, there is a significant difference between historical importance and the actual viewing experience. Just because a film was revolutionary at the time does not automatically mean that it continues to work equally well decades later. My verdict: Star Wars (1977) is undoubtedly an important piece of film history, but personally, I find it to be a film whose age is impossible to overlook in many respects. The repetitive action, occasionally simplistic lightsaber duels, inconsistent pacing, excessive dialogue, and visual presentation that is no longer particularly impressive prevent me from feeling any genuine enthusiasm. What was once celebrated as a cinematic spectacle now feels rather ordinary in many moments and even downright boring at times. I can certainly appreciate what this film has accomplished for the history of cinema, but that does not mean I have to consider it a timeless masterpiece. A milestone of its time – but by no means, in my opinion, a masterpiece that has stood the test of time. //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////// Star Wars (1977) – Ein Meilenstein der Filmgeschichte, der aus heutiger Sicht deutlich an Glanz verliert Star Wars aus dem Jahr 1977 mag Filmgeschichte geschrieben und ein ganzes Genre nachhaltig geprägt haben, doch bei einer heutigen Betrachtung fällt es zunehmend schwer, die damalige Begeisterung uneingeschränkt nachzuvollziehen. Was seinerzeit als revolutionäres Science-Fiction-Abenteuer galt, wirkt aus heutiger Sicht stellenweise erstaunlich antiquiert, langatmig und wenig abwechslungsreich. Natürlich muss man dem Film seinen historischen Stellenwert zugestehen, allerdings schützt auch dieser nicht vor einer kritischen Bewertung seiner zahlreichen Schwächen. Beginnen wir mit dem wohl bekanntesten Element des Films: dem Soundtrack. Die ikonische Filmmusik ist zweifellos ein Klassiker und gehört längst zur Popkultur. Allerdings ist sie mittlerweile derart omnipräsent, dass ihre Wirkung zumindest bei mir deutlich nachgelassen hat. Man hat das Gefühl, diesen einen musikalischen Leitgedanken mittlerweile rund um die Uhr um die Ohren zu bekommen. Was einst unverwechselbar und beeindruckend war, wirkt inzwischen beinahe überstrapaziert. Auch die technische Präsentation hinterlässt einen durchwachsenen Eindruck. Die Bildauflösung wirkt teilweise mangelhaft, und die veraltete Schnitttechnik trägt zusätzlich dazu bei, dass manche Szenen künstlich in die Länge gezogen werden. Gerade im Vergleich zu modernen Filmproduktionen fällt auf, wie sehr sich die filmischen Möglichkeiten weiterentwickelt haben. Was 1977 noch als spektakulär galt, insbesondere die Explosionen und Weltraumschlachten, löst heute kaum noch Begeisterung aus. Vieles wirkt schlicht überholt und kann mit aktuellen Produktionen visuell nicht mehr mithalten. Besonders enttäuschend ist für mich die Action. Die Weltraumschlachten folgen häufig demselben Muster und wiederholen ein nahezu identisches Szenario, wodurch sich schnell ein Gefühl der Monotonie einstellt. Gleichzeitig fehlt es an Abwechslung und wirklicher Dynamik. Die Lichtschwertkämpfe sind ebenfalls weit davon entfernt, mit modernen Choreografien zu konkurrieren. Sie wirken banal, unbeholfen und stellenweise beinahe uninspiriert. Hinzu kommt, dass die Action trotz ihrer überschaubaren Menge teilweise erstaunlich unübersichtlich inszeniert ist. Es entsteht ein merkwürdiger Widerspruch: Der Film bietet mir insgesamt zu wenig Action, schafft es aber gleichzeitig nicht immer, die vorhandenen Actionszenen überzeugend und nachvollziehbar zu präsentieren. Ein weiterer Kritikpunkt betrifft das Erzähltempo. Dieses schwankt teilweise erheblich zwischen überhasteten und unnötig langatmigen Passagen. Spannende Situationen werden gelegentlich viel zu schnell abgehandelt, während andere Szenen durch ausgedehnte Dialoge und wenig relevante Momente unnötig gestreckt werden. Besonders die übermäßige Screentime von C-3PO und R2-D2 fällt dabei negativ auf. C-3PO verliert sich immer wieder in langatmigen Monologen, die den Erzählfluss eher ausbremsen als bereichern. R2-D2 wiederum trägt mit seinem permanenten Piepen und seinen wiederkehrenden Lautäußerungen nicht unbedingt dazu bei, meine Geduld aufrechtzuerhalten. Was vermutlich als humorvolle Auflockerung und charakteristische Eigenheit gedacht war, entwickelte sich für mich zunehmend zu einem akustischen Geduldsspiel. Generell fällt auf, dass der Film spannende Situationen nicht immer mit der nötigen Konsequenz auflöst. Statt wirklicher Spannung und packender Inszenierung bekommt man gelegentlich erstaunlich banale Lösungen präsentiert. Auch die teilweise sehr explizite Darstellung bestimmter Szenen lässt erkennen, dass der Film aus einer anderen filmischen Epoche stammt. Das ist nicht grundsätzlich schlecht, macht sich im direkten Vergleich mit heutigen Sehgewohnheiten jedoch deutlich bemerkbar. Natürlich wäre es unfair, Star Wars ausschließlich an modernen Blockbustern zu messen und dabei seinen historischen Kontext vollständig auszublenden. Der Film hat zweifellos Maßstäbe gesetzt, die technische Entwicklung des Kinos beeinflusst und ein außergewöhnliches Franchise hervorgebracht. Doch zwischen historischer Bedeutung und persönlichem Filmerlebnis besteht ein erheblicher Unterschied. Nur weil ein Film seinerzeit revolutionär war, bedeutet das nicht automatisch, dass er auch Jahrzehnte später noch uneingeschränkt funktioniert. Mein Fazit: Star Wars (1977) ist zweifellos ein bedeutendes Stück Filmgeschichte, für mich persönlich jedoch ein Film, dessen Alter sich an vielen Stellen nicht mehr übersehen lässt. Die repetitive Action, die teilweise banalen Lichtschwertkämpfe, das schwankende Erzähltempo, die übermäßigen Dialoge und die heute nur noch bedingt beeindruckende visuelle Präsentation verhindern, dass bei mir echte Begeisterung aufkommt. Was damals als cineastisches Spektakel gefeiert wurde, wirkt heute in vielen Momenten schlicht gewöhnlich und stellenweise sogar langweilig. Ich erkenne durchaus an, was dieser Film für die Filmgeschichte geleistet hat, aber ich muss ihn deshalb noch lange nicht für ein zeitloses Meisterwerk halten. Ein Meilenstein seiner Zeit – aber für mich keineswegs ein Meisterwerk, das den Zahn der Zeit unbeschadet überstanden hat.

Admittedly, I have been avoiding the Star Wars universe ever since I was first exposed to the franchise in 2011 and I have turned down opportunities to watch the movies, even though sitting through them would finally grant me the authority to speak on why they are bad. I respect the influence of the franchise, but no amount of cultural imprint can salvage dialogue this flat or a script this profoundly brain-numbing. I understand the intention to make dialogue sound “otherworldly” but there is no rule dictating that cynical delivery must also be this uninspiring and one dimensional: „When I left you I was but the learner. Now I am the master“. What’s most bothersome is the plot, which within its predictability lacks subtext, and relies entirely on archetypes compromising any potential for psychological depth. The black-and-white moral framework is tiresome and frankly I struggle to understand how people enjoy this spoon-fed narrative: „If you strike me down I shall become more powerful than you can possibly imagine“. A film that operates entirely on the surface, and fails the Bechdel test spectacularly. Pass.

Star Wars is a cultural phenomenon masquerading as a film — a genre picture of the highest order that has been mythologized into a sacred text by generations of sick, over-caffeinated fans who cannot distinguish between nostalgia and quality. George Lucas did not "save cinema" with this; he invented a template — the Hero's Journey as a fill-in-the-blank worksheet — and poisoned the well for every screenwriter who came after, flattening narrative complexity into a three-act diagram that now suffocates originality in every studio lot in Hollywood. The "revolutionary" special effects are now unwatchable — **clunky motion-control shots, painted matte backgrounds, and a Death Star that looks like a Space Age coffee table — but that is almost secondary to the fundamental problem: the film is morally binary to the point of Aesop-fable. There are no grey areas. The Rebellion is good, the Empire is evil, and the "Force" is a vague spiritual hand-wave that functions as a deus ex machina and a moral compass simultaneously, resolving every ethical dilemma with a hand-wave and a glow. Lucas replaces philosophy with mysticism, politics with archetypes, and character with costume. Carrie Fisher's Princess Leia is not a "strong female character" — she is a damsel in distress who is captured, tortured, and rescued by a farm boy in the same act, and the film apologizes for none of this. Her iconic hairstyle is the only "subversive" element in a **role that is structurally identical to a Disney princess minus the singing. Harrison Ford's Han Solo is a cliché so pure it is W.C. Fields-esque — a bumbling, roguish, ultimately redeemable scoundrel who never has a moment of genuine moral complexity. And Peter Mayhew's Chewbacca is a comic-relief sidekick with zero dialogue and zero interiority, a tall, furry punchline that exists to validate the "buddy" trope and fill screen time. The dialogue is agonizingly expository: Mark Hamill's Luke Skywalker explains the plot to himself in clunky, on-the-nose monologues that assume the audience cannot be trusted to infer a single thing. The "I love you" / "I know" exchange between Leia and Luke is the most baffling line of dialogue in the history of cinema — a non-sequitur that means nothing and serves no purpose beyond **proving that Lucas **could not write a simple "I love you" without making it sound like a Star Trek transporter malfunction. The "I don't like sand, it's coarse and gritty and gets everywhere" line is not "charming" — it is a screenwriter who does not understand why characters should ever explain their own preferences to the audience.

Commercialized Cinema: " Star Wars "  is the epitome of the commercialization of cinema: a product designed for mass consumption, whose cultural significance is inseparable from its immense commercial machinery . What is sold to the audience is not merely another film, but an entire universe of merchandise, video games, books, spin-offs, and endless sequels and prequels, entirely new series that go in-depth of seemingly uninteresting and quite unimportant characters. Even nostalgia itself becomes a commodity: The childhood memories associated with these films are repackaged and sold back to the very people who grew up watching them, encouraging a perpetual cycle of braindead consumption in which one is expected to keep buying, keep watching, and keep waiting for the next instalment. Art is reduced to a marketable franchise, and the audience to a consumer: it's goal is passivity and achieving stupidity. The irony is that even the supposedly "profound" political message of the original trilogy is rather superficial. Superficial indeed: "The Empire" can be interpreted as a representation of American imperialism, Nazi Germany, or the degeneration of a nominally democratic republic into authoritarian rule. There is, admittedly, something vaguely anti-imperialist in this narrative. The audience, i.e.  the consumers kind of get it, but those topics are largely a " Nebensache ." At the same time those themes remain largely schematic, stripped of any meaningful historical or political complexity. Oppression is embodied by an unmistakably evil Empire -- embodied by the evil Sith! -- , resistance by a virtuous rebellion -- and surviving Jedi --, and the conflict between them is resolved through a familiar struggle between good and evil… or hate and peace . Most of the times the political messaging remains largely a "Nebensache"; a minor subject, in the front remains the seeling of a product called " Star Wars. " And the story itself? A young boy called Luke is discovered by a quasi-magical space wizard i.e. Jedi. Luke learns that he possesses a mysterious connection to an ancient power i.e the "force," and eventually discovers that he is destined to play a decisive role in restoring balance to the universe. It is an archetypal hero's journey, very standard children heroic story, built upon the most familiar conventions of mythological storytelling. The prequels complicate this mythology with increasingly convoluted explanations, but complexity should not be confused with depth, or any consistency. Beneath the elaborate universe, the seemingly millennial of history, the story itself, the core of this entire awful franchise of consumption product, remains remarkably trite: It is dusty, conventional storytelling dressed up in the aesthetics of a "space blockbuster." And, to be fair, it works perfectly well as a children's adventure. That is precisely the point! Of course, one will inevitably be told that "Star Wars" is a children's film, as though this observation were somehow a sufficient defence against any criticism. It is true that a work intended for children need not be philosophically sophisticated, and children's cinema is perfectly capable of addressing complex moral, social, and political questions. The problem is not that " Star Wars " is a children's film, but that its defenders so often seem unwilling to acknowledge the limitations of what they are defending. Much of the franchise's cultural prestige appears to rest less on the intrinsic qualities of the films than on the emotional attachment audiences have developed to them. Ultimately, "Star Wars" represents the negation of art through its subordination to the logic of commodification!

“Star Wars” (1977) feels completely divorced from the larger media franchise that spawned.  I see a very sweaty, desperate passion project made within the limitations of 70s sensibilities and production capabilities– and at times it does have an endearing, oddball charm as a dated genre picture. The prequels and Disney's later commercial bloat might as well exist in a different realm. Lucas’ visual compositions really stimulate my eyeballs, and he knows how to exploit the great production design– every single interior within the Empire makes for an iconic fantasy world with striking pseudo-architecture. I still like the scene where Luke stares at the twin suns setting over the desert, yearning for a higher calling. ODD STORY STRUCTURE -At first you think that the droids are going to be the protagonists–at least until you past the 20 minute mark. -Luke completes his arc around that certain tragic event at the midpoint, and from there the only thing left is to get better at The Force. -Han has an arc that extends into Act 3. -I’m okay with all of these things. PROBLEMS The storytelling comes off as clunky–I’m thinking of the exposition dump with Luke’s aunt and uncle at dinner, which kind of rushes through information about the wider world and Luke's desire to go to an academy. Obi-Wan gives more exposition dumps. Some scenes are too fast, others things are way too slow, and the story progression feels sloppy and haphazard at times. Act 3 feels incomplete. Now, I know this was written as part of a trilogy. But, I needed a little more meat on the bone for this first installment. Maybe two more scenes at the end could have given Han and Luke each a proper stopping place.

George Lucas’ Star Wars is a highly polarising film for me; while I deeply respect its craft and history, I cannot bring myself to fully connect with the narrative and characterisations, both of which I find subpar and basic. I want to first highlight the cinematography, which is absolutely astounding. Whether through Lucas’ masterful use of colour, spatial geometry, blocking, or lighting, this film is genuinely impressive visually. This is even more remarkable considering it was released in 1977, making the film an incredible technical feat in cinema. Likewise, the puppetry and set design are masterclasses in their own right. The way Lucas creates such gripping locations and iconic characters is highly respectable. Star Wars establishes a beautiful sense of atmosphere and represents the absolute elite tier of cinematic craftsmanship. However, while the film is undeniably iconic and a major cinematic feat, I cannot bring myself to care for its characters and narrative. Yes, characters like Luke, Leia, Han, C-3PO, and Vader are some of the most universally recognised figures in cinematic history, but that does not make them particularly nuanced. I often find that Lucas relies far too much on traditional morality—a flaw that seems inevitable given the clear division between the dark and light sides, and the heavy colour symbolism of the lightsabers. I find this approach far too simplistic and emotionally hollow. Lucas constructs these characters to be so morally juxtaposed that he leaves the audience no space to ponder their psychology or philosophy; they merely represent the symbolic divide between good and bad. Real morality, however, does not work like that; it is filled with nuances and flaws—something Lucas rarely explores. While I completely understand that he was trying to make a populist franchise that appealed to a broad audience, I constantly find myself questioning his choice to create such vague, hollow characters just to manipulate mainstream emotions through a simplistic divide in characterisation, which feels cheap and unrealistic. The same can be said about the film's plot, which is nearly identical to Akira Kurosawa’s The Hidden Fortress. The narrative feels far too predictable and derivative, playing out as a conventional hero’s journey and a rise against evil while offering nothing psychological or profound. It is designed purely as entertainment and populist media. This is evident through Lucas’ heavy reliance on fight scenes and special effects, which, while visually interesting and perhaps entertaining for some, rarely provide anything profound to the plot. Instead, they merely act as a way to show off the film's technical expertise and manipulate the emotions of a mainstream audience. The primary reason this film (and the original trilogy as a whole) falls short of being a masterpiece becomes clear when comparing it to the work of Akira Kurosawa, by whom Lucas was deeply inspired. This influence is inevitable in the film's craftsmanship, as Lucas frequently draws parallels to Kurosawa through wide location shots and the strategic use of weather. However, what differentiates the two—and proves that Kurosawa remains significantly superior—is that Kurosawa was not afraid to create philosophical, dark endings, detestable protagonists, or sympathetic villains. Lucas, by contrast, rejects the very ethos that made Kurosawa a pioneering director, condensing the morality so that it can be understood even through the lens of a child. Lucas stripped away the exact elements that made Kurosawa a genius just to conform to a mainstream Western audience that demands clear narratives and characterisations. What frustrates me so much is that while Kurosawa may not be as famous as Lucas in the West, he was certainly far from niche and was deeply mainstream in Japanese culture. This makes it even more confusing that Lucas felt the need to dilute this ethos so drastically, given that it had already proven successful in the Japanese market. Ultimately, this leaves the original Star Wars feeling like a beautifully crafted but soulless clone of various Kurosawa classics—designed as populist fiction rather than pure, philosophical art.

Millennium Condor, Chico, la VF de ce film est une ode aux arguments de Regelegorila. Dans Star Wars, épisode IV : Un nouvel espoir (1977), réalisé par George Lucas, la galaxie est sous le joug de l'Empire galactique, dirigé par le redoutable Dark Vador. Lorsqu'une jeune princesse, Leia Organa, transmet les plans de l'Étoile de la Mort, une arme capable de détruire des planètes, ceux-ci tombent entre les mains de Luke Skywalker, un jeune fermier vivant sur Tatooine. Accompagné de Han Solo, Chewbacca et Obi-Wan Kenobi, Luke rejoint l'Alliance rebelle dans une mission périlleuse pour détruire cette arme et mettre fin à la domination de l'Empire. Alors oui, le film est ultra culte, oui, la musique de John Williams est mythique, oui, les décors sont magnifiques, oui, l'univers construit autour de Star Wars est exceptionnel, mais moi, je n'adhère pas. Je trouve que le film est mal écrit. C'est un simple appel à l'aventure : faut sauver la princesse. C'est vraiment pas ouf, ultra classique, comme on en a vu et lu des centaines depuis des siècles, sans parler du manichéisme primaire : les méchants de l'Empire, les gentils rebelles. Il avait quel âge, Lucas, quand il a écrit le film ? Mais pire que ça, il y a énormément de situations totalement connes, comme cette fois où le groupe sort du compacteur à ordures. Han Solo a un blaster et un groupe de cinq ou six stormtroopers débarque. Han Solo tire et en tue un, mais au lieu de tirer sur Han Solo, Luke et Leia, les stormtroopers fuient. MAIS PUTAIN NON. En fait, George Lucas a mis un tel plot armor sur les protagonistes que tu te retrouves dans des situations absurdes. C'est très, très mal écrit. À de trop nombreuses reprises, les personnages sont à quelques mètres des ennemis et LA TOTALITÉ des tirs adverses finissent 15 mètres à côté. Qu'on soit bien d'accord, je ne nie pas du tout l'impact de la saga. Je dis juste que les défauts du film sont ceux qui font que, moi, je n'adhère pas. Cette écriture d'enfant me fait tiquer toutes les cinq minutes. Difficile de rester concentré, difficile de suspendre mon incrédulité. Au final, Star Wars est impressionnant sur énormément de points, mais les défauts d'écriture font que, moi, je n'accroche pas du tout. C'est un excellent film pour les fans, mais pas pour moi.

I get that, for its time, it probably worked, and if I'm being honest, when I watched this as a kid, I had no complaints. I thought it was really cool. Unfortunately, revisiting it as a grown man, it just didn't evoke the same emotions it once did. However, the world of Star Wars will forever be cool to me. The Rebellion, the Empire, and everything surrounding them are still incredibly fascinating, which is why, despite my many gripes with this film, I could never bring myself to hate it. There's still some genuinely great material here, particularly the dynamic between Obi-Wan and Luke Skywalker, as well as Luke's early scenes on Tatooine, which I think are among the film's strongest moments. I do think the film drags in places, but overall, it's a serviceable introduction to what would eventually become one of the most iconic franchises in all of media.

Rewatching this almost 50 years after its release made me realize how good A New Hope actually is. Sure, some aspects haven’t aged particularly well. The pacing can feel a little slow, the action sequences are noticeably dated, and the lightsaber duel between Obi-Wan and Vader feels almost ridiculous compared to what the saga would eventually become. But the storytelling? Still works incredibly well. The world-building, the characters, John Williams’ iconic score, and the classic Hero’s Journey structure are all fantastic. George Lucas didn’t just create a science fiction adventure. He laid the foundation for one of the greatest cinematic universes ever made. I still think The Empire Strikes Back takes everything this film established to a much higher level, especially in terms of dramatic conflict and emotional depth. But revisiting where it all began gave me a whole new appreciation for it. A film that shows its age, but never loses its magic. May the Force be with you. Always.

Uma das melhores criações de mundo de todos os tempos. Ter assistido isso em 77 deve ter sido uma experiência de outro planeta. O figurino, a maquiagem, a direção de arte. Tudo isso ajuda a construir um cenário que nenhuma franquia que até hoje não conseguiu igualar. A trilha sonora, Meu Deus. Está no maior pedestal de Hollywood. John Williams incomparável. E os personagens são muito icônicos. A introdução de cada um deles é uma aula para qualquer um. Nenhum deles fica abaixo. Geral é absurdamente carismático. Acho que o ritmo no segmento de Tatooine deve incomodar quem já conhece a franquia. Para quem está começando a ver Star Wars, acho que existe uma criação de universo bem forte ali. Para mim que já assisti todos os live-actions, é uma parte um pouco cansativa. O resto do filme, por outro lado, tem um ritmo perfeito. Ação que não para e muito charme em tela. Absolutamente todas as interações entre os personagens são incríveis. E nada de tempo sendo perdido. Lógico que George Lucas não tinha como prever o sucesso de sua história e todo o material que seria criado depois. Mas infelizmente, a falta de conexão com produções cronologicamente anteriores da franquia, seja por meio de eventos ou até o tom, me frustrou um pouco. Ainda mais tendo acabado de assistir Andor e Rogue One . A atmosfera aqui é muito mais leve. A ameaça do império e de sua arma destruidora de planetas nem parece tão intimidadora como outras obras nos fizeram imaginar. O filme sofre sim com a falta de recursos do seu tempo em várias sequências, não tem como negar. Mesmo assim, é surpreendente demais o que conseguiram fazer com o que estava disponível. Tem cenas em que o visual não perde em nenhum aspecto para algumas produções da Disney de anos recentes. Enfim, é um clássico absoluto e atemporal.
